title: The effect of Relativistic Aberration on Cosmological Distances

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (4) is written as z := (λ0-λ)/λ = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)), but the standard relativistic Doppler relation is 1+z = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)) (i.e. λ0/λ = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β))). Inverting Eq.(4) as literally written gives β=(z²-1)/(z²+1), which contradicts Eq.(5) (β=[(1+z)²-1]/[(1+z)²+1]) that the paper itself derives from Eq.(4) 'by reversing the relationship'. Eq.(5) can only be obtained if the correct relation 1+z = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)) is used, not z = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)) as printed. The subsequent aberration equations (11)-(12), which give ϵ=(1+z)ϵ', are also only consistent with the correct (1+z) relation, confirming Eq.(4) as printed is inconsistent with the rest of the paper's own derivations.

The paper refers to the maximum mass limit for neutron stars as the 'Volkov-Oppenheimer limit.' The correct and widely used name for this limit is the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) limit. This is a factual naming/attribution error regarding a well-established physical concept.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.3, paragraph on the age of the Universe
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims 'the age of Universe vary very little with the variation of cosmological parameters and depends strongly only on H0, as shown in (Carroll et al. 1992).' This misrepresents Carroll, Press & Turner (1992), whose central point (and a classic result in cosmology) is that t0·H0 varies substantially with ΩM and ΩΛ (e.g., from 2/3 for ΩM=1,ΩΛ=0 to ~0.96 for a ΛCDM-like universe), which was historically used to resolve the 'age problem' via a nonzero cosmological constant. The claim that age depends 'strongly only on H0' and varies 'very little' with ΩM/ΩΛ contradicts the well-known content of the cited paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Text following Equation (30), derivation of the Etherington relation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'Substituting equations 21 and 28 in it... we immediately obtain the Etherington relation' (Eq. 31: d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A). However, substituting Eq. (21) dS_G=r_G²dΩ_G and Eq. (28) dS_O=r_O²(1+z)²dΩ_O into Eq. (30) (dS_G dΩ_O = dS_O dΩ_G(1+z)^2) yields r_G = r_O(1+z)^2, which combined with Eqs. (24) and (29) gives d_L/d_A=(1+z)^3, not (1+z)^2 as claimed in Eq.(31). Only substituting the earlier, uncorrected definition Eq. (26) (dS_O := r_O²dΩ_O) instead of Eq.(28) reproduces the stated Etherington relation (1+z)^2. This reveals an internal inconsistency between which equation (26 vs 28) is actually used to recover Eq.(31).

Equation (34) contains the term sqrt((1+z)^2(1+ΩM z) - z(2+z)ΩΛ), but the function H(z',ΩM,ΩΛ) defined in Equation (36), which is supposed to represent the same quantity (as used later in Eqs. 35, 37, 39, 40), is written as (1+z'^2)(1+ΩM z') - z'ΩΛ(2+z'), i.e., with '1+z'^2' instead of '(1+z')^2'. These two expressions are mathematically different and inconsistent with each other and with the standard Friedmann-equation-based formula from Carroll et al. (1992) that the paper claims to follow.

predicted_errors.error_location: Footnote 1 (discussion of Von Laue 1931 / Pauli & Sparzani 2008)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The author admits the cited source attributing a key physical result (p·R=const in RW metric) to Von Laue (1931) is 'practically unobtainable' and that he 'searched for it for months and found nearly nothing,' yet still presents partial, unverified bibliographic details and relies on this unverifiable attribution to support a foundational claim used throughout the paper. Using/propagating an unverifiable citation for a load-bearing physical result is a citation integrity issue.

The text states: 'the effect on the surface area of every point of the CMB is increasing it by 10^6, while the temperature anisotropies of the CMB are in the order of 10^-6 K.' This juxtaposes a dimensionless geometric scaling factor (10^6, from (1+z)^2 with z≈1000) against a temperature anisotropy magnitude in Kelvin (10^-6 K), implying a meaningful numerological connection between two physically unrelated and dimensionally different quantities without any derivation connecting them, which overstates the significance of the coincidence.

The text states: 'Equation 5 clearly doesn't hold if the expansion of the Universe between us and the CO is faster than c, but in that case we simply can't detect any light signal from the CO so the problem doesn't arise.' This conflates the special-relativistic relative velocity (restricted to β<1 in Eq. 5) with the cosmological recession velocity in comoving coordinates, which standard cosmology shows can exceed c for observable objects (e.g., objects beyond the Hubble sphere remain observable, as established in the literature on misconceptions about superluminal recession, e.g. Davis & Lineweaver 2004). The claim that superluminal recession implies no observable light signal is not generally correct in standard FLRW cosmology.
